title: The blind turtle
hookLine: a turtle surfacing once a century through a yoke adrift on the ocean: human birth is that rare (SN 56.48)

lines: AN OCEAN, A YOKE, A TURTLE.
IN THE BOOK OF THE FOUR TRUTHS.
cards: The odds of a particular person being born are hard to even write down. Your parents had to meet, on that day, and their parents before them, back through every war and famine and missed train.
People like to play with those numbers. The Buddha played with them too, only without numbers. He used an ocean, a wooden yoke with a single hole, and a turtle who can't see.
It's a strange picture, and it sits in the book of the four truths for a reason.

teach.b: Here's the picture, from the Connected Discourses. Suppose someone threw into the great ocean a yoke, the wooden collar you'd put on an ox, with a single hole in it.
And in that ocean a blind turtle comes up to the surface once every hundred years. Would the turtle, coming up, push its neck through the hole? Only after a very long time, the monks say, if ever.

The neighboring sutta makes the scene bigger. Suppose the whole earth were one sheet of water. The east wind pushes the yoke west, the west wind pushes it east, the north wind south, the south wind north.
It would be by chance, the monks say, that the turtle's neck went through.

teach.h: THAT HARD TO BE BORN HUMAN.
teach.b: Just so, the Buddha says, it's by chance that someone is born human, by chance that a Buddha appears, by chance that the teaching shines in the world. And now all three have happened.
Then the point lands: so effort should be made to understand this is dukkha, this is its arising, this is its ending, this is the way.
The turtle isn't there to make anyone feel lucky, or anxious. It's there to make this hour feel valuable.
Teachers, especially in Tibetan traditions, call it a precious human life: the time, the senses and the freedom to hear the teaching and practice it.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says it plainly: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals." Different schools read rebirth in their own ways.
The sutta's own point is urgency.

how: In Tibetan traditions especially, practitioners often reflect on the precious human life at the start of practice, sometimes recalling the image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

o: a fishing boat lost in a storm at sea
a turtle, the picture of a rare birth
a wooden yoke drifting on the sea

games.q: match the pieces of the turtle sutta.
p: one hole, pushed by the four winds
a human birth is that rare
make an effort to see the four truths

s: the turtle story is told to make people feel anxious
it's there to make this hour feel valuable, and to urge the four truths.
the sutta ends by urging effort to understand the four truths
that's why it's in the book of the truths.
the turtle surfaces once every year
once every hundred years, and it's blind.

games.q: the Buddha asks: a blind turtle surfaces once a century. what are the odds it puts its neck through a single drifting yoke? what do you say?
o: very slim; only after a very long time.
games.why: the monks say it might happen only after a very long time; the Buddha says a human birth is that hard to come by.

practice: Feel that you're here, breathing, hearing, able to think, and picture the wide gray ocean, the yoke drifting, and a turtle rising, just once, into the light.
Breathe in, knowing you have this breath; breathe out, knowing it won't come again in quite this way. Don't hurry to use the hour well; just feel what it's worth.

wordCard.voice: Kacchapa, the turtle. The Buddha's picture of how rare a human birth is: a blind turtle surfacing once a century through a single drifting yoke.

orig.note: Pali kacchapa: a turtle or tortoise; the sutta's blind turtle is kāṇo kacchapo.

carryVoice: Your line: rarer than the turtle. This hour is part of that rare life. Day three hundred forty-seven, done.
